summary: Sets out requirements for a generic route-tracing tool and the protocol behind it. Operators would use it to check that IP forwarding works properly. It goes beyond traceroute, which finds the path between two interfaces, by also revealing details of the tunnels that carry traffic along that path.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine following a trail of footprints to see where a friend walked. Traceroute shows the stops along the way. This idea would also show the secret tunnels the friend slipped through that you could not see before.

subtitle: Requirements for a traceroute tool that can see through tunnels

tldr.problem: The classic traceroute tool shows which routers are on the path between two addresses, but it cannot see inside tunnels. Some tunnels appear as a single hop, others as multiple hops without indicating they are part of a tunnel. Operators need to diagnose tunnel failures and understand the full path.
tldr.mechanism: A generic route-tracing application would send probes and receive detailed responses that reveal not just the router hops, but also tunnel types, tunnel endpoints, tunnel components and their delays, and the MTU at each step. It would support multiple tunnel types: GRE, MPLS, IPsec, GMPLS, IP-in-IP, and L2TP.
tldr.outcome: Operators could verify IP forwarding and diagnose faults through tunnels. This memo specifies requirements for the application and the protocol that would support it, setting the stage for better network debugging.

facts.label: Tunnel types supported
facts.value: GRE, MPLS, IPsec, GMPLS, IP-in-IP, L2TP

today: RFC 3609 is Informational and describes requirements rather than a complete protocol. These requirements have influenced ongoing work in network diagnostics and tunnel visibility tools, though no single standard implementing all of them has become universal.

sections.title: Why Tunnels Need Special Tracing
sections.content:
Tunnels are a powerful way to carry traffic through networks. An IP tunnel wraps IP datagrams inside other datagrams, hiding the inner network. MPLS Label Switched Paths tunnel traffic by adding labels. GRE, IPsec, L2TP, and GMPLS all tunnel traffic for different purposes.

The problem is that traceroute, the standard tool for discovering the path through an IP network, cannot see inside tunnels. Depending on how the tunnel is configured, traceroute might show the tunnel as a single hop (when the tunnel does not copy the TTL from the inner header to the outer header), or it might show many hops without indicating they are inside a tunnel (when TTL is copied). Either way, an operator loses visibility into the tunnel itself.

This memo specifies what a better generic route-tracing application must do: discover the forwarding path, reveal tunnel details when permitted, show tunnel types and endpoints, and help diagnose broken tunnels.
sections.plainLanguage: Tunnels hide what is inside them. When your traceroute tool goes through a tunnel, it either shows nothing or shows many stops without saying they are inside a tunnel. You need a tool that says where the tunnel is and what is happening inside it.

sections.title: Application Requirements
sections.content:
The memo lists 15 detailed requirements for the tracing application. Key requirements include:

Security awareness: The application must support a security token that identifies the tracer's privileges. Network elements will use this to decide whether to reveal tunnel details or hide them from unauthorized parties.

In-line and third-party traces: An in-line trace discovers the path from the host running the tool to any interface in the network. A third-party trace discovers the path between any two interfaces, and does not require running the tool on a router in the path. Unlike existing tools, it should not rely on IP options (which change how the network forwards the datagram) or SNMP access.

Tunnel visibility: When tracing through a tunnel, the user can choose to see the tunnel as a single hop or in detail (revealing tunnel type, name, identifier, endpoints, and component details with round-trip delays). The application must support nested tunnels (for example, IP-in-IP over MPLS) and multiple tunnel types: GRE, MPLS, IPsec, GMPLS, IP-in-IP, and L2TP.

Robustness: The tool must work even when some routers do not support the protocol, and provide useful information about partial paths through broken tunnels. It must also display the MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) at each interface, which is important for diagnosing fragmentation issues.
sections.plainLanguage: The tool needs to ask permission to peek inside tunnels, trace from anywhere to anywhere without needing to sit on a router, show you the tunnel details if you have permission, and tell you what went wrong even if the path is broken.

sections.title: Protocol Design Principles
sections.content:
The protocol uses a simple probe-and-response model. The tracing application sends a probe, and each hop in the path responds with details about itself. This is stateless—each hop does not need to remember previous probes—and uses UDP for transport.

Why stateless: Stateless operation prevents denial of service attacks where an attacker floods the network with probes, and allows the protocol to scale to millions of probes without overwhelming individual routers.

Why UDP: The protocol needs a stateless transport. ICMP was rejected because carrying MPLS label information in an ICMP datagram would violate the ISO layer model. Plain IP was rejected to conserve protocol identifiers. UDP sits at the right level and provides the needed statelessness.

Routing requirements: The device running the tool must have IP routes to the tunnel ingressess it is tracing. All devices in the path must have routes back to the tracer so they can send responses. This is a practical constraint that makes the protocol work in real networks.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol asks one question per probe and gets one answer back, without needing to remember anything. This keeps it simple and fast, and uses UDP, which works well for quick questions and answers.

sections.title: Security and Access Control
sections.content:
The application is designed with access control in mind. A configurable policy determines what information each user can see. The policy requires user identification and authorization before granting access to tunnel details or control plane information.

The protocol itself must be resistant to abuse. It must not create security holes, consume excessive resources (CPU or bandwidth), or be exploitable by attackers launching denial of service attacks or replaying old messages. The stateless design helps here: because each message is independent, there is no session state to corrupt or hijack.

The security token mentioned in the application requirements provides a way to encode authorization information in each probe, so that intermediate routers can make access control decisions without needing to maintain per-user state.
sections.plainLanguage: Only people with permission can see tunnel details. The protocol should not let attackers crash routers or trick them into answering the same question twice.
